01Rationale

Why this level matters

Agents can now take on routine work across the back office and the front desk. The skill that matters is choosing the right process, connecting it safely to your software, keeping a person in charge of what counts, and measuring what it saves.

02Target competencies

Intended learning outcomes

Pick the right process

Choose work worth automating, and work that should stay with people.

Build an agent

Create an agent that completes a business task with tools and approvals.

Connect your tools

Link AI models, APIs and business software so work flows without copying.

Run it safely

Add logs, limits and handover so you can trust it and fix it.

Proposed scope: 16 lessons in 4 modules

This outline describes the intended curriculum. Lesson materials and assessments are not yet available.

Module 1Foundations

What agents can and cannot do.

  1. What an agent is, in plain terms
  2. Choosing processes worth automating
  3. Approvals, limits and risk
  4. Measuring time and cost saved

Module 2The back office

Routine work that eats the week.

  1. Automating accounting tasks

Module 3Connect and grow

Module 4Running it

  4. Your automation plan

04Planned practical work

One process, automated end to end

Proposed project: Automate a real process from your own work, with a person approving what matters. This practical component will be developed and validated before the level opens.

The steps

  1. Describe the process and its steps
  2. Decide what the agent may do and what needs approval
  3. Build the agent and connect one tool
  4. Test it on ten real examples
  5. Add a log and a handover
  6. Measure the time saved and write the runbook

Intended validation criteria

  • There is an approval before any irreversible action
  • Every run is logged
  • You can state the time saved per week

05How you learn

Proposed learning design

Worked examples

The professional academies begin with complete examples and make the reasoning behind good decisions visible.

Guided practice

Scaffolds fade as learners progress—from annotated examples to structured tasks and independent work.

Retrieval and review

Low-stakes questions prompt recall; review revisits important concepts. Model answers and rubrics make improvement specific.

Research-informed updates

The academies cite primary research and standards, record review dates and receive versioned updates as evidence changes.

The proposed learning design draws on retrieval practice, worked examples and spaced review; detailed learner materials will be published before release. Read the evidence and sources.

06Intended audience

What you need

No programming needed. You should know how your own business or team runs.
